initial_observation.demographics: A girl in her early adolescence
initial_observation.encounter_context: referred to our clinic for evaluation
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: presenting with a 2-year history of multiple pinpoint sized wheals with surrounding 1–3 cm erythematous flares developing immediately after contact with water
presenting_symptoms: multiple pinpoint sized wheals with surrounding 1–3 cm erythematous flares developing immediately after contact with water
lesions occurring immediately after water exposure irrespective of temperature or source including showering, bathing, swimming pools, seawater, and rain
each episode lasted approximately 30–60 min and resolved spontaneously
no symptoms due to sweat or tears exposure
symptomatic episodes when in contact with animal saliva
known_prior_history: no significant medical history other than known allergies to dust, rabbits and cats
no systemic reactions such as headache, shortness of breath, wheezing, dizziness or fainting
no other forms of inducible urticaria
no skin reactions in family members when exposed to water
symptoms not linked to consumption of food or medication prior to water contact
no use of estroprogestins or hormonal medications

evidence_items.source_text: On physical examination, skin appeared clear with a distinct absence of dermographism.

A routine laboratory evaluation was performed, encompassing a complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, urine analysis, panels for immunoglobulins, thyroid function tests, all yielding results within normal limits, ruling out any underlying abnormalities.

After discontinuing antihistamines for 1 week, a water provocation test was administered. This involved regional contact using a damp cloth on the patient’s trunk, maintained at 35°C (figure 1A). After 20 min, there was a development of urticarial eruption on the trunk, which was consistent with the patient’s natural exposure to water (figure 1B).
Given the patient’s history and the results of the water provocation test, a diagnosis of aquagenic urticaria was established.

On evaluation at our clinic, cetirizine, a second-generation H1 antihistamine, was prescribed at 10 mg daily, leading to further symptom relief. Following this, the use of montelukast was discontinued, and the patient continued to experience substantial relief from the wheals.
At the 8-month follow-up, she did not report any further episodes of symptoms, unless a dosage of cetirizine was missed.

At the 14-month follow-up, the patient continued to report further improvement in her condition, which enabled her to participate in daily activities without any restrictions. Additionally, the administration of the Children’s Dermatology Life Quality Index yielded a score of 0, indicating no impairment of quality of life-related to her condition at this time.
